# The Problem This System Is Solving

Every year, the Global Monitoring Database (GMD) team at the World Bank ingests
hundreds of household survey datasets from countries around the world. Each survey
is different. Different countries use different questionnaires, different variable
names, different coding schemes, and different ways of categorizing the same
underlying concepts. Consider something as simple as gender. One survey codes it as 1 and 2, with labels
in Portuguese. Another uses the strings "M" and "F". A third records it as 0 and 1
with no labels or documentation at all. Each dataset is capturing exactly the same
underlying concept; none of them looks the same to a computer, or to an analyst trying
to combine them. Now extend that challenge to education levels, employment status,
household relationships, urban or rural location, and dozens of other variables, across
surveys from scores of countries conducted over decades. Before any of this data can be used for
international comparisons of poverty, welfare, or living standards, it must be
*harmonized*, meaning converted into a single, standardized format that allows meaningful
comparison across countries and years.

Harmonization is expert work. It requires an analyst to read the survey documentation,
understand what each variable in the raw data actually measures, and then write a
transformation script (typically in the statistical programming language Stata) that
converts each raw variable into its GMD equivalent. For a single survey, this process
can take days. For a database that handles hundreds of surveys per year, the cumulative
burden is enormous.

The challenge is compounded by the fact that harmonization decisions are often not
formally documented. They live in scripts, in email threads, in the memory of
individual team members. When a team member leaves, or when a survey needs to be
re-harmonized years later, the reasoning behind past decisions is difficult to recover.
Errors are hard to audit. Inconsistencies across surveys are hard to detect.

The AI-assisted harmonization system is built to address exactly this.

---

# What the System Does, and What It Does Not Do

Before describing how the system works, it is important to be clear about what it
does and does not do.

The system **does** read survey documentation and raw data, reason about how each
raw variable maps to the GMD standard, and produce a structured draft of the
harmonization decisions. It draws on past decisions to inform its reasoning. It checks
its own work against formal rules before presenting it for review.

The system **does not** make final decisions. Every mapping it proposes must be
reviewed, approved, and signed off by a human expert before it is ever executed.
The system is designed to accelerate and standardize the *first draft*, not to replace
judgment. The human reviewer remains the methodological authority.

This distinction runs through every design choice in the system, from how the AI is instructed to how its outputs are stored.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Harmonization Specification**

The central artifact of this system is a document called the Harmonization
Specification. It is a structured, machine-readable file (formatted as JSON, a
standard data exchange format) that records, for every variable in a survey, exactly
what transformation is proposed: which GMD variable it maps to, what recoding is
needed, what confidence level the AI assigned, and what reasoning was used. This
document is what the human reviews and approves. Nothing is executed without an
approved Specification.
:::

The current phase of development focuses on a proof of concept scoped to non-welfare
demographic variables: gender, age, education, urban and rural classification,
household relationships, and labor force status, across approximately 100 to 200 new
surveys per year. This scope is deliberate. These variables are complex enough to
stress-test the methodology and bounded enough to allow careful evaluation before
extending the system to more sensitive variables such as welfare aggregates
(consumption and income estimates), where methodological errors carry greater
consequences.

# The Four Permanent Input Sources

The system draws on four sources of information that are always present, regardless
of which survey is being harmonized. Three of them grow richer over time as the system
learns.

## Raw microdata

This is the actual survey dataset, the file that contains one row per household or
individual, with columns for each variable. It typically arrives as a Stata `.dta`
file, though CSV and other formats are also supported. The raw microdata is the ground
truth of what was actually recorded in the survey.

The raw microdata is stored securely in a centralized file storage system (Azure Blob
Storage) where all pipeline components can access it. Crucially, the raw microdata is
never sent to the AI system directly. Instead, it is first processed into a structured
summary (described in the next section), and only that summary reaches the AI.

## Survey documentation

This includes any documentation that came with the survey: questionnaire PDFs,
codebooks in Excel or Word format, interviewer manuals, variable lists, or any other
reference material that explains what the survey variables mean. In the ideal case,
this also includes a **DDI file**.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**DDI: Data Documentation Initiative**

A DDI file is a structured, machine-readable XML file that contains standardized
metadata about a survey: variable names, question text, response categories, universe
descriptions (who was asked each question), and survey methodology notes. It is the
international standard for documenting household survey data. Many surveys archived
in the World Bank's Microdata Library have DDI files available via a public API.
Where a DDI exists, it is the richest and most reliable source of documentation for
the system.
:::

Not all surveys have DDI files. Many arrive with only a PDF questionnaire or an
unstructured codebook. This is precisely why the documentation parsing stage (described
below) exists: to extract and structure whatever documentation is available into a
consistent format the AI can use.

## Historical decisions database

This is the system's institutional memory. It contains structured records of every
harmonization decision that has ever been made and approved within the system:
which raw variable was mapped to which GMD variable, what transformation was applied,
what situation was declared (direct mapping, inferred mapping, not mappable), and any
notes the reviewer added.

Over time, this database tends to become the most valuable input source of all. It encodes
decades of expert judgment in a form the AI can search and reason with. The database
is initially seeded from legacy Stata harmonization scripts using a purpose-built tool
called **do2screen**, described in the next section.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**do2screen**

`do2screen` is a Stata `ado` program developed by the GMD team that reads a Stata
harmonization script (a `.do` file) and extracts, in structured form, the
transformation decisions it encodes: which variables were recoded, how, and from
what source. This makes it possible to convert years of existing harmonization work
into structured records that can populate the historical decisions database, without
having to re-document everything manually.
:::

One practical implication of this design is worth noting upfront: in the system's
early life, the quality of its AI drafts depends directly on how thoroughly the
historical database has been seeded. An empty or sparse precedent base gives the AI
little to draw on. This is why converting legacy harmonization scripts via do2screen
is not a one-time setup task but a foundational investment in the system's early
performance, and why it happens before the pipeline begins processing new surveys.

The historical database uses a technology called a **vector database**, which allows
the AI to retrieve relevant past decisions through similarity search rather than exact
matching. When the AI is reasoning about an education variable with an unusual coding
scheme, it can ask the database: *"Find me past decisions about education variables
from surveys with similar characteristics"* and retrieve the closest matches,
even if no exact precedent exists.

## GMD schema and guidelines

This is the authoritative definition of every GMD target variable: its name, label,
valid values, data type, and derivation rules. It is stored in a structured relational
database and is the final authority in all cases of conflict. If a historical precedent
suggests something that contradicts the GMD schema, the schema always wins. The
schema database is what ensures that no matter how many different surveys the system
processes, all outputs conform to the same standard.

---

# Stage One: Pre-Processing, Converting Everything to Structured Schemas

The fundamental principle underlying the entire system is this: **no downstream stage
should ever receive unstructured input.** The AI drafting stage should not try to read
a raw PDF. It should not try to interpret a Stata binary file. It should receive only
clean, consistently structured data that has already been organized into
a well-defined template. The job of the pre-processing stage is to make this happen.

Pre-processing has two parallel tracks that run simultaneously.

## The data profiling track

The data profiling step reads the raw microdata file and computes a comprehensive
structured summary of what it contains. This step is entirely automated. No AI is involved.
It is, in essence, a sophisticated version of what a data analyst would do when first
exploring a new dataset: running `codebook` in Stata, or `str()` and `summary()` in R.

The output is a **data profile schema**, a structured JSON document that contains,
for every variable in the dataset:

- The variable name and any embedded label
- The data type and storage class (numeric, string, byte, integer, float, and so on)
- Summary statistics for numeric variables (mean, standard deviation, minimum,
  maximum, percentiles)
- The count of missing values and the missing rate
- For categorical or string variables: the number of distinct values and a frequency
  table of the most common values
- The total number of observations in the dataset

This profile tells the AI what the data actually looks like in practice. The picture
it provides can differ significantly from what the documentation says. A codebook might list
a variable as having five response categories; the actual data might contain three,
or seven, or include unexpected codes that indicate data quality issues. The profile
captures reality.

## The documentation parsing track

Simultaneously, the documentation parsing step processes any available survey
documentation. Unlike data profiling, this step is AI-assisted: it uses a language
model to read unstructured documents and extract their content into a structured format.

The reason AI is needed here is that survey documentation varies enormously. One
survey's codebook is a tidy Excel table. Another's is a scanned PDF of a paper
questionnaire from 1998. A third is a Word document with inconsistent formatting and
embedded footnotes. A purely mechanical parser would fail on many of these. A language
model can read them all and extract the same kinds of information regardless of format.

The output is a **documentation schema**, another structured JSON document that
captures, for every variable mentioned in the documentation:

- The question text as it was asked
- The list of response categories and their numeric codes
- The universe: who was asked this question (all adults, only employed individuals,
  households with children, and so on)
- Any notes or caveats from the questionnaire
- The section of the questionnaire where the variable appears

When a DDI file is available, the documentation parsing step reads it directly.
DDI files are already structured and can be parsed more reliably. When no DDI exists,
the AI extracts what it can from whatever documentation is available.

::: {.callout-important appearance="simple"}
**A valuable byproduct: synthetic DDI creation**

When a survey has no DDI file, the documentation schema produced by the parsing step
is rich enough to serve as one. The system stores it back into the documentation
database, effectively creating a synthetic DDI for the survey. Over time, this means
the system is not only harmonizing surveys but also building out documentation
coverage for surveys that were previously underdocumented. For the GMD team, which
intends to create DDIs for new harmonized surveys, this is the natural mechanism for
doing so.
:::

---

# Stage Two: AI Drafting, Reasoning Toward a Harmonization Specification

Once both pre-processing tracks are complete, the AI drafting stage begins. This is
where the intelligence of the system is concentrated.

The AI receives four inputs simultaneously:

1. The **data profile schema**: what the raw data actually contains
2. The **documentation schema**: what the survey documentation says the variables mean
3. **Relevant historical decisions**: retrieved from the historical database by
   searching for past decisions about similar variables and similar surveys
4. The **GMD schema**: the authoritative definitions of all target variables

Working with these four inputs, the AI reasons about each variable in the survey and
proposes a mapping to the GMD standard. For each variable, it must answer a set of
questions: Does this variable correspond to a GMD target variable? If so, which one?
Is the mapping direct (the values need no transformation) or does it require recoding?
Are there any complications a human reviewer should know about, such as unexpected
values, missing documentation, or ambiguous categories?

For each variable, the AI assigns one of three mapping situations. **Situation A** is
a direct mapping: the raw variable corresponds cleanly to a GMD target variable and
its values require little or no transformation. **Situation B** is an inferred mapping:
the underlying concept is present in the survey but requires a country-specific
conversion rule, for example, translating a national degree classification into
standardized years of schooling, or recoding a local employment category into the GMD
labor force scheme. **Situation C** means the variable cannot be reliably mapped; it
is flagged as not mappable and will be set to missing in the output, with the reason
documented. This three-way classification is recorded in the Harmonization
Specification for every variable in the survey.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**RAG: Retrieval-Augmented Generation**

RAG is the technical term for the mechanism by which the AI searches the historical
database before generating its proposals. Rather than relying purely on its general
training, the AI first *retrieves* the most relevant past decisions from the historical
database and then uses those as context when *generating* its draft. This is what
allows the system to reflect the GMD team's specific institutional conventions and
past choices, not just general statistical knowledge.
:::

The AI does not simply produce one draft and stop. It operates in an internal
**sandbox loop**: it generates a draft specification, runs internal consistency checks
against the GMD schema, identifies any contradictions or obvious errors, revises its
proposals, and repeats until its own tests pass. Only then does it present the draft
to the human reviewer. This means the reviewer receives a draft that has already
passed a first round of automated quality checks, not a raw, unvetted output.

The result of this stage is the **Harmonization Specification**: a structured JSON
document listing every variable-level mapping decision, the AI's confidence level, its
reasoning, and the historical precedents it drew on. This document is saved to
centralized storage where the Review Application can read it.

---

# Stage Three: Human Review, Where Judgment Is Applied

The Harmonization Specification is a machine-generated proposal. Nothing in it has
authority until a human expert reviews and approves it. This is not a formality; it
is the methodological core of the system.

When a new draft Specification is saved to storage, the reviewer is automatically
notified and opens it in the **Review Application**: a purpose-built web interface
that presents the draft in a readable, interactive format. The reviewer sees, for each
variable, the source variable and its documentation, the proposed GMD target, the
AI's reasoning, and the historical precedents cited. They can approve the mapping as
proposed, reject it and send it back to the AI with written feedback, or annotate it
with caveats and corrections before approving.

The Review Application reads from and writes back to the same centralized storage that
the rest of the pipeline uses. It is the only point in the system where a human
directly interacts with the pipeline's state.

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
**The rejection loop**

When a reviewer rejects a mapping, the rejection is not simply discarded. It is sent
back to the AI drafting stage as structured feedback: what was wrong, why it was
rejected, and what the reviewer expects to see instead. The AI revises the relevant
portions of the specification and resubmits for review. This loop can repeat as many
times as necessary. Every revision and the reasons for it are logged in the audit
trail.
:::

When the reviewer is satisfied with the full Specification and approves it, the
approved version is saved back to storage. This triggers the next stage automatically.

---

# Stage Four: Execution, Turning Decisions into Data

The execution stage takes the approved Harmonization Specification and implements it
on the raw microdata. This stage is entirely **deterministic**: it involves no AI, no
probabilistic reasoning, and no judgment. It is code that reads a specification and
applies it precisely.

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**Deterministic code**

Deterministic means that given the same inputs, the code always produces exactly the
same output. There is no randomness, no model inference, no approximation. An approved
Specification, applied to the same raw data file by the execution engine, will always
produce the same harmonized dataset, whether on the first run, on the hundredth run, or
five years from now. This reproducibility is essential for a system that feeds official
statistics.
:::

The execution engine reads the approved Specification, loads the raw microdata, and
applies each transformation in sequence: renaming variables, recoding values,
computing derived variables from atomic inputs, and applying any filters or conditions
specified. It does not interpret the Specification; it executes it exactly as written.

This strict separation between the *decision* (made by the AI and approved by the
human in the Specification) and the *execution* (performed mechanically by the engine)
is one of the most important design choices in the system. It means that every
harmonization output is fully explainable: anyone can look at the approved
Specification and the execution log and understand exactly what happened and why,
without having to reason about what an AI "might have been thinking."

---

# Stage Five: Quality Assurance, Automated Validation

Before any output is considered final, it passes through an automated quality
assurance stage. The QA engine compares the harmonized dataset against the GMD schema
to verify that every output variable falls within its defined valid range, has the
correct data type, meets completeness requirements, and is internally consistent with
related variables.

Examples of checks performed: Is the age variable non-negative and within a plausible
range? Do the education category codes match the GMD enumeration exactly? Is the
urban/rural indicator binary with no missing values above the acceptable threshold?
Are household-level and individual-level variables consistent with each other?

If all checks pass, the output moves to the final stage. If any check fails, the
failed output is not stored as final; instead, it is flagged and sent back to the
human review stage with a detailed report of which checks failed and why. The reviewer
then determines whether the issue lies in the Specification (requiring a revision) or
in the raw data (requiring a note in the output documentation).

---

# Stage Six: Outputs and the Learning Loop

A harmonized survey that passes QA produces two categories of output.

The first is the **harmonized GMD dataset** itself: a clean, standardized microdata
file in which all variables conform to the GMD schema, ready for integration into the
database. This file is accompanied by a complete **audit trail**, a permanent,
immutable record of every decision made during the harmonization process. It captures what inputs
were used, which version of the Specification was approved, who approved it and when,
what the QA results were, and any revisions or annotations made during review.

The audit trail means that the question *"How was this variable harmonized, and why?"*
can always be answered precisely, not from memory, but from a permanent, queryable record.

The second output is less visible but equally important: the **save-back to the
historical decisions database**. Every approved harmonization decision (every
variable mapping that passed review and QA) is stored back into the historical
database as a new precedent. The next time the system encounters a similar survey, it
will have this decision available as a reference.

This is how the system improves over time. Early in its life, it draws on legacy Stata
scripts converted via do2screen. As it processes more surveys, it accumulates a richer
and richer base of vetted decisions. The quality of its drafts improves. The reviewer's
workload decreases. The gap between what the AI proposes and what the human would have
decided independently narrows.

This learning loop is not automatic in the sense of unsupervised machine learning:
no decision enters the historical database without human approval. Every precedent in
the database has been validated by a domain expert. This is what makes the
institutional memory trustworthy.

---

# The Infrastructure Underneath

All of the above requires a set of cloud infrastructure components to function. These
are described in detail in the accompanying *Infrastructure Requirements* document
prepared for ITS. In summary, the system relies on seven components:

| Component | What it does |
|-----------|-------------|
| **File storage** (Azure Blob Storage) | Holds all raw files, processed schemas, approved specifications, and outputs |
| **Rules database** (Azure SQL) | Stores the canonical GMD schema, always the final authority |
| **AI language model** (Azure OpenAI Service) | The engine behind documentation parsing and AI drafting |
| **Historical decisions database** (Azure AI Search) | Stores and retrieves past harmonization decisions via similarity search |
| **Compute environment** (Azure Kubernetes Service) | Runs all pipeline jobs on demand, with team-managed deployment |
| **Audit trail and monitoring** (Azure Monitor) | Records every system action for accountability and debugging |
| **Review Application** (Posit Connect or Azure-hosted) | The web interface through which human reviewers interact with the pipeline |

: Infrastructure components {tbl-colwidths="[35,65]"}

The most critical infrastructure question, and the one that must be resolved before
any other design can be finalized, is whether **Azure OpenAI Service** is approved
for use in the World Bank Group's Azure tenant. This is the enterprise version of the
AI language model, designed to meet the data residency and security requirements of
organizations like the World Bank. Without it, the documentation parsing and AI
drafting stages cannot function as designed. All other questions are secondary to this
one.

---

# The Role of Schemas: The Real Design Challenge

It might be tempting to think of this as primarily an AI system, but that framing
misses the point. It is, at its core, a **schema design system** in which AI plays a supporting role.

Every stage of the pipeline is, at its core, a conversion from a less structured form
to a more structured one:

- Survey documentation (unstructured PDF) → Documentation schema (structured JSON)
- Raw microdata (binary Stata file) → Data profile schema (structured JSON)
- Both schemas, combined with rules and precedents → Harmonization Specification (structured JSON)
- Approved Specification → Harmonized GMD data (structured dataset)

The quality of the AI's output is directly proportional to the quality of the schemas
it receives as input. A vague, inconsistently defined documentation schema produces
vague AI proposals. A precisely defined schema, in which every field has a clear
meaning and every value has a constrained range, produces consistent, auditable
proposals.

This means that before any code is written and before any AI is prompted, the team
must carefully define:

1. **The data profile schema**: exactly what fields the automated profiling step
   produces for each variable
2. **The documentation schema**: exactly what fields the documentation parsing step
   extracts from questionnaires and codebooks
3. **The Harmonization Specification format**: exactly what fields and values are
   valid for each variable-level mapping decision

These three schemas are the contracts between pipeline stages. Getting them right is
the highest-leverage design work in the project.

---

# What This Means for the GMD Team in Practice

For a harmonizer working with this system, the day-to-day experience changes in a
specific and bounded way. The mechanical first-draft work (reading documentation,
proposing mappings, and writing transformation logic) is handled by the system. The
harmonizer's time is redirected toward the work that requires genuine judgment:
reviewing proposals, catching edge cases the AI missed, annotating unusual situations,
and making the final call on ambiguous mappings.

The save-back loop means that every judgment a harmonizer makes is preserved
permanently, attributed to them, and available to inform future work. Over time, the
team builds not just a database of decisions but a structured record of *reasoning*:
why a particular approach was chosen for a particular kind of survey, what the known
complications are for specific country contexts, how the team has resolved recurring
ambiguities in the past. This institutional knowledge, which today lives largely in
individual memories and scattered scripts, becomes a shared, searchable, durable
resource.

For the proof of concept, the system covers the demographic variable categories
described in Section 2. Welfare aggregates remain out of scope until the proof of
concept demonstrates that the methodology is sound.

---

# Summary

The GMD AI-assisted harmonization system is best understood not as an AI that
harmonizes surveys, but as a structured pipeline that converts unstructured inputs
into structured outputs at every stage, with human judgment applied at the decisive
moment before any transformation is executed.

A new survey arrives. Its raw data is profiled automatically. Its documentation is
parsed by an AI agent into a structured schema. Both schemas, together with the GMD
rules and years of historical decisions, are handed to an AI drafting agent that
proposes a complete Harmonization Specification. That Specification is reviewed and
approved by a human expert using a purpose-built review interface. Once approved, a
deterministic execution engine applies the Specification to the raw data. Automated
quality checks validate the output. The final harmonized dataset, complete with a full
audit trail, is stored. And the approved decision is saved back into the historical
database, making the system incrementally smarter for the next survey.

The system does not remove expertise from harmonization. It amplifies it, by encoding
past expertise into a form that can inform future work, and by redirecting current
expertise toward the decisions that actually require it.
